title: The Battle Begins (Days 1–10)
body:
PART VII: THE 18-DAY KURUKSHETRA WAR

The Battle Begins (Days 1–10)

न काङ्क्षे विजयं कृष्ण न च राज्यं सुखानि च ।
किं नो राज्येन गोविन्द किं भोगैर्जीवितेन वा ॥

Translation: I do not desire victory, O Krishna, nor kingdom, nor pleasures. Of what use is kingdom to us, O Govinda, or enjoyment, or even life itself? (Bhagavad Gita 1.32)

The grand war of Kurukshetra, the cosmic laboratory of Karma and Dharma, erupted with the shattering blare of conches and the thunder of eighteen Akshauhini divisions. The battlefield became a dense, terrifying arena where the physical limitations of the material plane (Prakriti) clashed with the relentless, unbending laws of cosmic justice. On the first morning, Dushasana took command of the vanguard of the Kaurava army, marching like death incarnate, while Bhimasena, the colossal embodiment of wind-like strength, stood at the head of the Pandava host.
During the initial ten days, Pithamaha Bheeshma directed the Kaurava forces as their Supreme Commander, raging across the holy plain of Kurukshetra like a consuming fire. His movements were so rapid that to the bewildered Pandava soldiers, he appeared to multiply into hundreds of Bheeshmas, laying waste to their ranks. On the first day, the Pandavas sustained massive casualties; Prince Uttara, the son of King Virata, riding a majestic war-elephant, confronted Shalya and was impaled in the chest by a lethal javelin, falling lifeless to the earth. Uttara's brother, Sveta, went into a fierce rampage to avenge him, decimating Shalya's relief units and breaking Bheeshma's standard before Bheeshma himself, drawing his bow to his ear, pierced Sveta with a fatal, deep-striking arrow.
The unchecked onslaught of the Grandsire threw King Yudhishthira into deep despair. Sree Krishna, acting as the divine inner guide (Antaryaami), comforted the weeping king, reminding him of the great warriors in his ranks. On the third day, Bheeshma arrayed the Kauravas in the Garuda Vyuha (Eagle Formation), which Arjuna countered with the Chandra Vyuha (Crescent Moon Formation). Stung by Duryodhana's bitter accusations of harbouring affection for the Pandavas, Bheeshma fought with supreme, unparalleled heroism. When Arjuna, paralysed by deep-seated affection and reverence for his grandfather, held back his hand and discharged weak, hesitant arrows, Sree Krishna's righteous anger flamed up. To protect the path of Dharma, Sree Krishna threw down the chariot reins, leapt to the earth, and raised a broken chariot wheel, brandishing it like the Sudarshana Chakra, vowing to slay the Grandsire himself. Arjuna threw himself at Krishna's lotus feet, weeping and imploring the Lord not to break his sacred vow of non-combat, pledging to discard his attachment and execute his Kshatriya duty.
On the eighth day, the battle claimed Iravan, Arjuna's heroic son by the Naga princess Uloopi, who was slain by the giant Alambasa after a devastating struggle, leaving Arjuna heartbroken and questioning the very purpose of this bloody sacrifice. Finally, on the tenth day, the Pandavas executed a solemn strategy designed to release the Grandsire from his mortal bondage. Placing Sikhandin—who was born female and whom Bheeshma would never raise a weapon against—in front of Arjuna's chariot, they confronted Bheeshma. Recognising Sikhandin as the reincarnation of Amba, Bheeshma dropped his weapons and stood peacefully amidst the storm of battle. Screened by Sikhandin, Arjuna steeled his heart and discharged a torrent of sharp arrows that pierced the Grandsire's armour at every joint.
Bheeshma fell headlong from his chariot, his body so densely transfixed with arrows that it did not touch the earth, resting instead on a bed of honour formed by Arjuna's shafts. As the great veteran lay waiting for the auspicious northern solstice (Uttarayana) to let go of his life-breath, Arjuna materialised a cool stream of Patala-Ganga from the depths of the earth with the Parjanya Astra to quench his grandfather's thirst, leaving both armies in deep, silent reverence for the fallen patriarch.
